title: Continental breakup at the Flood
statement: Per the canon, the single continent the Elohim raised from the seabed was broken by the home-planet strike the canon identifies as the Flood: the blasts sent its fragments 'drifting outwards from the centre of the shock', swept the whole land surface, and buried the living matter — forests, animals, humans — 'immediately and all together' in a ring around the impact; the corpus reads today's continental configuration and its ongoing drift as the residue of that displacement, and the fossil-bearing strata as the burial sequence of what died when in the aftermath of the initial explosion, while accepting the planet's own deep age and registering, in its own voice, that mainstream plate tectonics and radiometric dating place the Pangaean breakup roughly 195 million years ago.

includes: The canonical layer, in two tiers of different standing (review 0001): (a) the message text — the single original continent raised by the creators and the later drift of its pieces (TBWTT ch. 2 ¶14), the Israel team's territory on 'the single continent' (¶28), and the home planet's decision to destroy all life on Earth by nuclear missiles (¶58); (b) the signed essay printed as chapter 4 of the canon's third book — Marcel Terrusse, chemical engineer and Raëlian guide, 'Raelism Through the Eyes of Science', §2 'A New Hypothesis for the History of Humanity' — which alone supplies the breakup of the continent, the fragments sent outward from the centre of the shock, the swept surface and the living matter buried at once in a ring, the residual velocity of the drift, the petroleum ring read as the burial's signature, the upheaval and the survivors' return (2005 English combined edition pp. 330–332; 1979 French text at LWTE-4:26–46, French column)

The corpus reading that rides on it: today's continents as the still-moving fragments; the fossil beds as the burial, their sequence read as the record of what died when in the aftermath of the initial explosion rather than as deep-time deposition; the tropical fossils under Antarctic ice and the petroleum ring as the corpus's stated correlates

The compressed dating the corpus assigns under the Model-C lattice: the continent raised in the Age of Sagittarius (woh-claim-0059) and broken at the opening of the Age of Gemini, c. 6,690 BCE (woh-claim-0010, woh-claim-0019)
The explicit acceptance of the planet's own age: the corpus disputes the timing of the continental and fossil record, not the roughly 4.5-billion-year age of the Earth
excludes: The Flood decision and its procedure, carried by woh-claim-0010, which deliberately excludes the geological consequence this record carries
Any mechanism reconciling radiometric and paleomagnetic ages with the compressed timeline; the corpus registers the discrepancy as an open question and this record does not resolve it

The number, yield, or location of the weapons, or the identification of specific impact sites; the source does not specify them and the corpus's petroleum-ring and crater-pattern remarks are correlates, not locators

Young-earth Flood geology as a position: the record registers that the corpus and the young-earth reading converge on the fossil beds as the signature of one catastrophe, but the corpus keeps an old planet, a recent and deliberate strike, and creators rather than a deity; the resemblance is not an adoption
The dating of the Flood itself beyond what the lattice supplies; the source gives no date, and the corpus's c. 6,690 BCE comes from woh-claim-0003 and woh-claim-0019

source_references.locator: Chapter 2 ¶14 (the seabed explosions that gathered the matter 'in the same place, which formed a continent'; 'originally there was only one continent on Earth', and 'all the continents which drifted apart fit together perfectly'); ¶28 (the Israel team's territory on 'the single continent'); ¶58 (the decision 'to destroy all life on Earth by sending nuclear missiles'); ¶64 (the radioactivity monitored and removed before disembarkation)

Chapter 4 ('Commentaries and Testimonials of Raelians'): Marcel Terrusse, 'Raelism Through the Eyes of Science', §2 'A New Hypothesis for the History of Humanity'. 2005 English combined edition pp. 330–332 — p. 331: the strike 'breaking up this original continent and sending each respective fragment drifting outwards from the centre of the shock', 'all the living matter including immense forests, animals and even Man' buried 'immediately and all together under tons of earth in a ring shape'; p. 330: the Nehring citation; p. 332: the upheaval and the survivors' return. 1979 French text, digitization French column LWTE-4:26–46 — n=26–30 and 38 the Nehring citation and the 'anneau pétrolier'; n=34–39 the strike, the swept surface, the burial 'sous des tonnes de terre', the fragmentation; n=40–41 the plates' brutal separation and the 'vitesse résiduelle' of present-day drift (absent from the English rendering). The digitization's English column (LWTE-4:35, 37, 43–44 as cited before review 0001) is the 2005 English text and is not paragraph-aligned with the French

p. 39 (the 'ring of oil': an oval band roughly 800 to 1,000 miles wide on the continental plates as reconstructed for 180 million years ago, holding nearly 85% of known petroleum resources and 210 of the 272 known giant fields; 'No complete explanation for this phenomenon is yet available'); Fig. 3.1, p. 40 (source: Dietz and Holden, 'The Breakup of Pangea', Scientific American, November 1970); title page and verso (R-2284-CIA, prepared for the Central Intelligence Agency under contract XG-4705). The study Terrusse's essay cites as a 'Hudson Institute' study by 'Professor Nehring'; the ring is Nehring's, the burial-rim reading is Terrusse's

GEN-WOH-1:9–10 (the waters gathered and the dry land appearing, read by the canon as the raising of the continent); 7:11 (the fountains of the great deep broken up, read as the impact-generated ocean displacement); 8:4 (the landing on the mountains of Ararat in the post-event configuration)

The founding text of young-earth Flood geology: the fossil-bearing strata as the deposit of one recent global flood — the reading the corpus converges with on the fossil beds and diverges from on the age of the planet, the mechanism, and the agent

Lyell's uniformitarian frame — present causes acting over deep time — from which the mainstream reading of the strata and of continental drift descends; the foil the corpus's catastrophic reading has to answer

The mainstream catastrophist literature's strongest late-Pleistocene impact proposal; establishes that recent continental-scale catastrophe is discussed within mainstream paleoscience while reaching nowhere near a continental breakup

A working geologist's case that the stratigraphic and fossil record cannot be the deposit of a single recent flood; the standing objection to any one-catastrophe reading of the strata, the corpus's included

alternatives.statement: Pangaea rifted roughly 195 million years ago by mantle convection; seafloor-spreading magnetic stripes, radiometric ages of oceanic crust, paleomagnetic reconstructions, and GPS-measured plate motion at steady centimetres per year describe continuous drift, not the decaying momentum of a single displacement.

The fossil succession is biostratigraphy laid down over hundreds of millions of years — faunal succession, radiometric calibration, and the absence of out-of-sequence assemblages — and cannot be the burial order of one event's aftermath.

The breakup-and-burial account is not in the message text: it is Marcel Terrusse's signed essay printed as chapter 4 of the third book (authorship settled by review 0001), and the 2005 French combined edition of the messages omits the chapter; the canonical core is TBWTT ch. 2 ¶14 and ¶58, which establish the single continent, the drift and the strike but not that the strike broke the continent. On this alternative a guide's essay printed with the message carries no canonical weight and the geological elaboration is early Raëlian apologetics; its one external citation is real (Nehring 1978) but describes a pattern on a 180-million-year plate reconstruction.

The reading reproduces young-earth Flood-geology arguments — rapid burial, petroleum from catastrophic burial, fossils as flood casualties — and inherits their documented failures, differing only in the agent and the date.

revision_triggers: The founder rules on the canonical weight of signed contributions printed with the messages, Terrusse's essay in particular; a ruling that they carry no canonical weight narrows this record's canonical layer to TBWTT ch. 2 ¶14 and ¶58 and moves the breakup reading to the corpus layer.
Collation against a 1979 first printing changes the essay's wording, or a reading of Dietz and Holden (1970) changes what Nehring's 'ring of oil' figure is based on.
Claim woh-claim-0010, woh-claim-0019, or woh-claim-0059 is revised or retired, or the Model-C lattice underlying the corpus's dating is reconciled differently.
The corpus adopts a stated mechanism for the discrepancy between radiometric ages and the compressed timeline; that would be a new record, not a revision of this one.
Public prose begins asserting a young planet, denying the breakup, or specifying impact sites and weapon counts, all of which this record excludes.
